克里特弓弦琴屬弦鳴樂器，發聲靠弓摩擦三弦，主要用於克里特島及多德卡尼斯群島、愛琴: The Cretan lyra is a chordophone, sounding when the bow rubs its three strings, and is used mainly in the traditional music of Crete, the Dodecanese and the Aegean islands, and also in parts of northern Greece. The old small lyra was used for dancing, and the loud type suits song accompaniment, while the common type is used in contemporary traditional performance. It can also appear in the performances of the rock singer Eric Burdon, and some players use it for Bach's cello suites.

The right hand bows while the left presses the strings with the side of the nail rather than pressing them against the fingerboard. The old lyra often left one string unfingered as a drone while the other two played the melody; the tuning was fifth, first, fourth, with the middle string lowest. The modern instrument is tuned in fifths, has no drone string, and all strings can be fingered for the melody. A beginner should first steady the instrument and the bowing hand, then practise pressing with the side of the left-hand nail and crossing strings.
克里特琴被視為中世紀拜占庭弓弦樂器的現存形式。九世紀波斯地理學家 Ibn Khu: The Cretan lyra is regarded as the surviving form of the medieval Byzantine bowed instrument. The ninth-century Persian geographer Ibn Khurradadhbih lists the lyra as a typical Byzantine instrument. Its westward spread is connected with the fifteenth-century Italian lira da braccio, and its descendants are seen in the Bulgarian gadulka, the Calabrian lira and the Istanbul kemençe. There are three accounts of its arrival in Crete: the Byzantine reconquest of 961, entry through Sitia before the twelfth century, or a gradual introduction with Byzantine music. In the Venetian period the violin influenced its tuning and playing; in 1920 the viololyra appeared, twenty years later the common lyra took shape, and in 1990 Ross Daly added the sympathetic strings of the Indian sarangi.

Its three strings, with the bowing, can produce delicate crescendos and diminuendos, and the range is wide and flexible. The pear-shaped soundbox gives a warm basic tone, which gives it a distinctive warmth. Compared with the sharp brightness of the Western violin, the Cretan lyra is gentler and more regional; compared with the soft drifting sound of the ancient harp, it is more penetrating and more dramatic. The tremor and mordent of the strings give it a song-like expressiveness, able both to present a light, nimble melody and to express deep grief, and it is the most affecting instrument of Cretan traditional music.

The Cretan lyra is a traditional three-string bowed instrument of the Greek island of Crete, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-71. The body is pear-shaped, the body and neck carved from one piece of seasoned wood, and the soundboard has two semicircular soundholes. It is held on the knee, the right hand bows, and the left presses the strings with the side of the nail rather than on the fingerboard. It is used in the traditional music of Crete, the Dodecanese, the Aegean islands and northern Greece, and is also regarded as the most widely played surviving form of the medieval Byzantine lyra.
琴身與琴頸由整塊陳木雕成，至少十年；傳統用克里特核桃、桑與當地懸鈴木，今多進口。: The body and neck are carved from a single piece of wood at least ten years old; traditionally Cretan walnut, mulberry and local plane tree were used, today mostly imported wood. The soundboard is straight-grained softwood, traditionally taken from seasoned building beams, ideally three-hundred-year-old beams from Venetian ruins. The old strings were of animal gut and the bow of horsehair, and the bow's arc once carried hawk bells; today a violin bow is mostly used. The source does not state the materials of the other parts, such as the sympathetic strings.
